t.1.71.1: Janamejaya said: Yayāti, our forefather, who was tenth in descent from Prajāpati, how did he obtain the daughter of Śukra, who was so exceedingly hard to win?
t.1.71.2: This I wish to hear in detail, O best of the twice-born; and tell me, in due order, of the founders of Pūru's lineage, each one separately.
t.1.71.3: Vaiśaṃpāyana said: There was a royal seer, Yayāti, whose splendor equaled that of the king of the gods. Śukra and Vṛṣaparvan both chose him, as it happened of old.
t.1.71.4: Since you ask, O Janamejaya, I shall relate to you that union of Devayānī and Yayāti, the son of Nahuṣa.
t.1.71.5: Between the gods and the asuras there arose a mutual conflict over sovereignty in the three worlds, with all their moving and unmoving beings.
t.1.71.6: Then, out of desire for victory, the gods chose the sage Āṅgirasa for the office of priest on behalf of those who sacrifice, while the others chose Kāvya Uśanas; those two brahmins were ever intensely rivalrous with each other.
t.1.71.7: There, those Dānavas whom the gods struck down when they met them in battle, Kāvya brought back to life again by relying on the power of his knowledge. Then they rose up once more and made war upon the gods.
t.1.71.8: But the gods whom the Asuras slew at the forefront of battle, Bṛhaspati of noble mind could not restore to life.
t.1.71.9: For he did not know that knowledge, the Saṃjīvanī, which the mighty Kāvya knew; and so the gods fell into the deepest despair.
t.1.71.10: Then the gods, agitated by fear of Uśanas Kāvya, approached Kaca, the eldest son of Bṛhaspati, and spoke to him.
t.1.71.11: Be devoted to us who are devoted to you, and render us the highest help. That knowledge which dwells in the brahmin Śukra of boundless splendor, bring it here quickly, and you shall have a share among us.
t.1.71.12: That twice-born one can be seen by you near Vṛṣaparvan. There he protects the Dānavas; he does not protect those who are not Dānavas.
t.1.71.13: You, being young, are able to win the favor of that sage, and of Devayānī too, the beloved daughter of that great-souled one.
t.1.71.14: You are able to win her favor; no one else is to be found who can, through virtue, courtesy and sweetness, through good conduct and self-restraint. For once Devayānī is pleased, you will surely obtain that knowledge.
t.1.71.15: Saying "So be it," Kaca, the son of Bṛhaspati, honored then by the gods, set out from there into the presence of Vṛṣaparvan.
t.1.71.16: Sent forth by the gods, O king, Kaca went in haste to the city of the lord of the Asuras, and on seeing Śukra he spoke these words.
t.1.71.17: I am the grandson of the seer Aṅgiras, the very son of Bṛhaspati himself, known by the name Kaca; may you accept me as your pupil.
t.1.71.18: I shall practise the highest brahmacarya with you as my guru; grant me your consent, O brahman, for a thousand years.
t.1.71.19: Kaca, may you be most welcome; I accept your words. I shall honor you, who are worthy of honor, and may Bṛhaspati be honored thereby.
t.1.71.20: Kaca said to him, "So be it," and took upon himself that vow, which had been enjoined by Śukra Uśanas, the son of Kavi, himself.
t.1.71.21: He undertook the vow for its appointed period, just as it had been prescribed, O Bhārata, all the while pleasing his teacher and Devayānī.
t.1.71.22: Always intent on winning her favor, the young man, standing at the threshold of youth, pleased Devayānī by singing, dancing, and playing music.
t.1.71.23: Attending upon Devayānī, a maiden who had reached the bloom of youth, he pleased her with flowers, fruits and errands done at her bidding, O Bhārata.
t.1.71.24: And Devayānī too, the charming young woman, singing to him, waited in private upon that brahmin, who faithfully kept his vows and observances.
t.1.71.26: Seeing him alone in a secluded spot in the forest, guarding the cows, the enraged ones slew him out of hatred for Bṛhaspati and also to protect their knowledge; and having killed him, they cut him into pieces as small as sesame seeds and gave him to the jackals.
t.1.71.25: Thus five hundred years passed there for Kaca as he kept his vow, and then the Dānavas came to know of that Kaca.
t.1.71.27: Then those cows returned without their herdsman to their own home; seeing the cows come back from the forest bereft of Kaca, Devayānī then spoke words at that time, O Bhārata.
t.1.71.28: Your agnihotra has not been offered, and the sun has set, O lord; the cows have come home without their herdsman, yet Kaca, father, is nowhere to be seen.
t.1.71.29: Clearly, father, Kaca has been slain or else has died. Without Kaca I would not live; I tell you the truth.
t.1.71.31: Then, employing the life-restoring knowledge, he summoned Kaca; thus summoned, Kaca appeared unharmed by virtue of that knowledge, and when questioned by the brahmin's daughter, he told her, "I was slain."
t.1.71.30: Śukra said: With the summons, "Here he is, come!" I bring the dead one back to life.
t.1.71.32: Once again, bidden by Devayānī, the brahmin went to the forest as it happened to gather flowers, and the Dānavas saw him there.
t.1.71.33: Then the Asuras, having killed him a second time, burned him and ground him to powder, gave him to the brāhmaṇa himself in his liquor.
t.1.71.34: Then Devayānī spoke once more to her father: "Father, Kaca, who gathers the flowers and carries out errands, is nowhere to be seen."
t.1.71.35: Śukra said: Daughter, Kaca, the son of Bṛhaspati, has gone the way of the dead. Though revived by my knowledge, he is slain like this again and again; what am I to do?
t.1.71.37: He whose grandfather is the most venerable Aṅgiras, and whose father is Bṛhaspati, rich in austerities, the son of a seer and the grandson of a seer as well, how should I not grieve for him, how should I not weep?
t.1.71.36: Do not grieve so, do not weep, Devayānī; one like you should not mourn for a mortal. The gods, the Viśvedevas, and the whole world bow to the change that comes upon them.
t.1.71.38: He was a brahmacārin, rich in austerity, ever diligent and skilled in his duties. I shall follow the path of Kaca and shall not eat, for handsome Kaca is dear to me, father.
t.1.71.40: Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Urged on by Devayānī, the great seer Kāvya, in great agitation, once again summoned Kaca, the son of Bṛhaspati.
t.1.71.39: Without doubt the Asuras hate me, they who slay my innocent disciple; these fierce ones wish to make me a non-brahmin, as indeed the Dānavas have set out to do. May there be an end to this evil here, for whom would the murder of a brahmin not burn, even Indra?
t.1.71.41: Afraid of his guru and summoned by the knowledge, he slowly spoke from within the belly. Śukra said to him: “By what path were you brought here, that you now dwell in my stomach? Tell me, O brahmin.”
t.1.71.42: By your grace my memory does not forsake me, and I remember everything that happened and how it happened. But so that my ascetic merit may not be wasted in this way, I endure this terrible torment.
t.1.71.43: O Kāvya, after killing me, burning me and grinding me to powder, the asuras gave me to you in your wine. While you stand firm, how could the magic of the asuras ever overcome the magic of a brahmin?
t.1.71.45: Two griefs like fire would burn me: the death of Kaca and the harm to you. In Kaca's death there is no peace for me, and if harm befalls you I am not able to live.
t.1.71.44: What that is dear to you shall I do today, child? Only by my death could Kaca have life. Kaca, who is within me, could not be seen except by the splitting open of my belly, Devayānī.
t.1.71.47: No one else could come forth alive again from my belly, save only a brāhmaṇa; therefore obtain the knowledge.
t.1.71.46: You have attained success, son of Bṛhaspati, since Devayānī loves you, her devoted one. Receive this life-restoring knowledge, if you are not Indra in the form of Kaca today.
t.1.71.48: Having become my son and been brought back to life, bring me back to life in turn, dear child, once you have come out of this body. Having obtained the knowledge from your guru and now possessed of that knowledge, you should look upon me with a righteous regard.
t.1.71.50: And Kaca, too, seeing that heap of holiness fallen dead, raised him up; having obtained that perfected knowledge, Kaca saluted his guru and then spoke to him thus.
t.1.71.49: Having obtained the knowledge from his teacher, the handsome brahmin Kaca split open the right side of the brahmin's belly and came forth, like the moon on the full-moon night at the close of the bright fortnight.
t.1.71.53: Then the illustrious Uśanas Kāvya rose up in wrath, wishing to do what was good for the brahmins, and, his suspicion aroused concerning the drinking of liquor, he himself spoke these words.
t.1.71.51: Those who do not honor the guru, who is worthy of worship, the giver of the unsurpassed truth, the treasure among the treasures of the four lines of tradition, go to evil worlds that have no firm footing.
t.1.71.52: Having been brought to deception through the drinking of wine, and likewise to a most dreadful loss of his senses, and seeing that Kaca, so handsome, had then been drunk down by one deluded by wine,
t.1.71.54: Any brāhmaṇa who from this day forth, dull-witted, drinks wine here out of delusion shall be one who has fallen away from dharma and is indeed a slayer of a brāhmaṇa; he shall be reviled in this world and in the next.
t.1.71.56: Having spoken thus, that great-souled one, the immeasurable treasure among treasuries of austerity, summoned those Dānavas, whose minds were bewildered by fate, and addressed these words to them.
t.1.71.55: Let the good brahmins who have listened to their teachers, the gods, and all the worlds hear this rule that I have established throughout the whole world, the boundary I have declared for the dharma of brahmins.
t.1.71.57: I tell you, Dānavas, you are fools! Kaca, now perfected, will dwell in my presence, having obtained the most precious Saṃjīvanī knowledge; he has become one with Brahman and is equal in power to Brahman.
t.1.71.58: Having lived in the presence of his guru for a thousand years, Kaca, granted leave, wished to go to the abode of the thirty gods.
